explanations.answer: They have not prevailed against Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the line, friend. Israel says, "…but they have not prevailed against me." (Psalm 129:2) Persecuted many a time, and still standing. Notice the "but" in the middle of that verse, because that little word is doing a LOT of heavy lifting.

I can see why that one tempts you after all those years of trouble. But the psalm says the opposite: "…but they have not prevailed against me." (Psalm 129:2) Nothing in the verse says Israel's spirit was broken. The song is a declaration, and it's a bold one.

explanations.answer: They drove Israel far from home
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like it could fit, but the psalm never says it. What Israel declares is, "…but they have not prevailed against me." (Psalm 129:2) The verse isn't about where Israel ended up. It's about who didn't win.

Ooh, I think the "short" slipped past you. The psalm says, "The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long." (Psalm 129:3) Long, not short. A long furrow means a long stretch of plowing, and I think that's the whole point of the picture.
You caught it, baker. The psalm says, "The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long." (Psalm 129:3) Long furrows, not short ones. One little word, and it changes the whole picture.

Yes, and listen to how plain it is. "The LORD is righteous…" (Psalm 129:4) After the plowmen and the long furrows, Israel doesn't grumble. Israel says who the LORD is. That's some steady faith right there.

I get the guess, because after a picture like that you'd expect a complaint. But the psalm says, "The LORD is righteous…" (Psalm 129:4) Israel turns from the plowmen and names the LORD as righteous. The song takes a turn, and that's the turn.

explanations.answer: Cut Israel from the cords of the wicked
explanations.explanation: That's it. "The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked." (Psalm 129:4) Cords are what tie something down, and the psalm says He cut Israel loose from them. The verse names the LORD as the One who did the cutting. I've been tied up in a few tight spots myself, so I know a good snip when I hear one.

explanations.answer: Taught Israel to plow its own fields
explanations.explanation: Plowing is in the psalm, but it's the plowmen doing it to Israel's back, not a lesson from the LORD. What Israel says He did is this: "He has cut me from the cords of the wicked." (Psalm 129:4) That plowing picture is the pain, not a skill. The LORD's part is the cutting.

explanations.answer: Told Israel to wait a little longer
explanations.explanation: Waiting is a fair thing to expect in a psalm like this, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, "The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked." (Psalm 129:4) The LORD's action there is a cut, and it's already done.

explanations.answer: That they be turned back in shame
explanations.explanation: Right on target. The psalm says, "May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame." (Psalm 129:5) It's a wish, not a report. Zion is the city of Jerusalem, and the ones who hate it are the ones in the wish.

explanations.answer: That they be welcomed into Zion
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, friend, but it's not what this psalm says. The wish is, "May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame." (Psalm 129:5) Turned back means sent the other way. No welcome mat in this verse.

explanations.answer: That they be made rulers of Zion
explanations.explanation: Nope, that would be a plot twist, and the psalm doesn't take it. It says, "May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame." (Psalm 129:5) Turned back, not promoted. Nobody in this verse is getting a crown.

Withers is the word. "May they be like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow…" (Psalm 129:6) The grass never gets the chance to grow. That's the picture the psalm wishes on those who hate Zion.

Drowning is a good guess for a plant, but it's not the word in the verse. The psalm says the grass "…withers before it can grow…" (Psalm 129:6) The verse says withers and says nothing about water. I wouldn't water a rooftop, and I don't think the psalm expects you to.

Freezing would make sense if the verse were about winter, but it doesn't mention cold. The psalm says the grass on the rooftops "…withers before it can grow…" (Psalm 129:6) Withering is the word the verse uses, not a deep freeze.

explanations.answer: The blessing of the LORD be on you
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The psalm says, "May none who pass by say to them, “The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD.”" (Psalm 129:8) So the wish is that no one passing by would speak that blessing over them. That's how the song ends.

explanations.answer: The LORD sees what you have done
explanations.explanation: That sounds like it fits the mood, but it's not in the verse. The psalm wishes that no one would say, "The blessing of the LORD be on you…" (Psalm 129:8) What's missing from the wish is a blessing, not a warning.

explanations.answer: You will never take Zion from us
explanations.explanation: I can hear why that one feels right in a song like this. But the psalm puts a blessing in the mouths of the passersby, or really, takes it out: "The blessing of the LORD be on you…" (Psalm 129:8) Nothing about taking Zion appears in that last verse.
